toc.text: Flow vs Apex: choosing the right motor
Building an end-to-end sync with retries
Orchestration recipe: quote to fulfilled order

html:
Automation is where CPQ goes from a quoting tool to a quote-to-cash pipeline. Salesforce gives you two complementary motors: Flow for declarative logic and Apex for heavy, transactional, or external work. Together with the trigger-handler pattern, platform events (Revenue_Sync__e), and HTTP callouts, they turn a quote into an order, a sync message into an ERP record, and a price check into a real-time external price. This guide shows you exactly when to use which tool, how to structure Apex so it stays testable, and how to integrate CPQ with systems outside Salesforce.

Learning objectives

  • Decide between Flow and Apex for a given CPQ automation requirement.
  • Apply the trigger-handler pattern so Quote triggers stay lean and testable.
  • Publish and subscribe to the Revenue_Sync__e platform event for quote-to-ERP sync.
  • Build HTTP callouts to an external pricing service and consume the response.
  • Combine flows and Apex services (QuoteCalculatorService, PriceRuleEngineService, OrderFulfillmentService) into an end-to-end integration.
  • Design retries, correlation IDs, and idempotent processing for integration events.
  • Handle the security and governor boundaries of callouts inside transactions.
  • Adapt the same patterns to RLM core objects (guide 11).

Finding the quote-to-cash automation points

Every phase of the lifecycle is an automation seam:

PhaseTriggerService / artifact
ConfigureProduct option selectionBundleConfigurationService
PriceLine added / quantity changedQuoteCalculatorService, PriceRuleEngineService
ApproveDiscount > thresholdApprovalRoutingService
ContractQuote approvedContractGenerationService
RenewContract nearing renewal dateRenewalQuoteService
FulfillOrder createdOrderFulfillmentService
BillSubscription activeBillingScheduleService
RecognizeBilling period closesRevenueRecognitionService
Sync outAny of the abovePlatform event Revenue_Sync__e -> ERP callout

None of these need to be one technology. Flows handle the orchestration; Apex services do the math and the network calls.

Flow vs Apex: choosing the right motor

CriterionFlowApex
Build speedFast, declarative, no deploy pipelineSlower, requires packaging/deployment
Complexity ceilingScreen steps, loops, record collectionsFull language: maps, exceptions, async
External callsExternal service steps (with limits)HttpCallout with full control
TransactionsOne transaction per flow executionFine control over save points and scope
Test coverageFlow coverage through test automation is optional-ish75% enforced on deploy/commit
Governance limitsFlow-specific limits (elements per run)Apex governor limits

Rule of thumb: use Flow for decision branching, record updates, and orchestration; write Apex for anything involving collections over many records, precise save ordering, custom error handling, or callouts that need retry/idempotency. In this codebase, the *Service classes (Apex) stay stateless and callable from either a Flow (via invocable methods) or a trigger-handler.

Tip: Prefer a small Flow that calls one Service method over a giant Flow with fifty decision elements. The codebase pattern is: trigger -> QuoteTriggerHandlerService -> domain service -> business result.

The trigger-handler pattern

Never put logic in the trigger body. Every trigger delegates to a handler:

apex
// Quote.trigger
trigger QuoteTrigger on Quote (before insert, before update, after insert, after update) {
    QuoteTriggerHandlerService.run(Trigger.operationType, Trigger.old, Trigger.new);
}

The handler keeps before/after concerns separate and only dispatches when relevant records actually changed:

apex
public inherited sharing class QuoteTriggerHandlerService {

    public static void run(System.TriggerOperation op,
                           List<Quote> oldList, List<Quote> newList) {
        switch on op {
            when BEFORE_UPDATE {
                updateTotals(newList);
            }
            when AFTER_UPDATE {
                List<Quote> changed = onlyChangedDiscounts(oldList, newList);
                if (!changed.isEmpty()) {
                    ApprovalRoutingService.route(changed);
                    publishSyncEvents(changed);
                }
            }
        }
    }

    static void updateTotals(List<Quote> quotes) {
        for (Quote q : quotes) {
            q.Total_ARR__c = q.QuoteLineItems == null ? 0 : q.Total_ARR__c;
        }
    }

    static List<Quote> onlyChangedDiscounts(List<Quote> oldList, List<Quote> newList) {
        Map<Id, Quote> oldById = new Map<Id, Quote>(oldList);
        List<Quote> result = new List<Quote>();
        for (Quote q : newList) {
            if (q.Discount_Percent__c != oldById.get(q.Id).Discount_Percent__c) {
                result.add(q);
            }
        }
        return result;
    }

    static void publishSyncEvents(List<Quote> quotes) {
        List<Revenue_Sync__e> events = new List<Revenue_Sync__e>();
        for (Quote q : quotes) {
            events.add(new Revenue_Sync__e(
                Source_Object__c = 'Quote',
                Payload__c = JSON.serialize(new Map<String, Object>{
                    'id' => q.Id, 'discount' => q.Discount_Percent__c
                }),
                Direction__c = 'Outbound',
                Status__c = 'Pending',
                Correlation_Id__c = based on quote Id,
                Integration_Type__c = 'QuoteToERP'
            ));
        }
        EventBus.publish(events);
    }

    static String based on quote Id { // correlation helper
        return 'Q2E-' + UUID arbitrary token derived from Id;
    }
}
Warning: the helper above is illustrative; generate correlation IDs with Crypto/UUID (or Id-derived deterministic keys) in real code so retries reuse the same Correlation_Id__c.

Platform events: Revenue_Sync__e

Platform events decouple Salesforce from downstream systems. Revenue_Sync__e has the fields you need for a resumable integration contract: Source_Object__c, Payload__c, Direction__c, Status__c, Correlation_Id__c, Integration_Type__c, Retry_Count__c, Endpoint__c.

Publishing is a single call, even for many events:

apex
List<Revenue_Sync__e> events = new List<Revenue_Sync__e>();
for (QuoteLineItem li : pricedLines) {
    events.add(new Revenue_Sync__e(
        Source_Object__c = 'QuoteLineItem',
        Payload__c = JSON.serialize(li),
        Direction__c = 'Outbound',
        Status__c = 'Pending',
        Correlation_Id__c = 'QLI-' + li.Id,
        Retry_Count__c = 0,
        Integration_Type__c = 'QuoteLineToERP'
    ));
}
EventBus.publish(events);
Tip: Payload includes all fields the consumer needs. Never publish a lookup Id and let the consumer re-query Quote over and over; that turns a decoupled event into a chatty call.

Subscribe with a Flow (Platform Events trigger) or an Apex trigger. A common pattern is a flow that inspects Status__c == 'Pending', invokes OrderFulfillmentService or the ERP callout service, and publishes a follow-up Revenue_Sync__e in the opposite direction once the ERP acknowledges.

HTTP callouts: external pricing

The second integration pillar is the callout. A classic use case: the ERP or custom pricing engine sets the authoritative net price. Exercise 12.2 (Call an External Pricing API) uses exactly this flow:

  1. A quote line is added or quantity changes (or a user clicks "Re-price externally").
  2. PriceRuleEngineService calls the endpoint defined in (or retried through) Revenue_Sync__e.Endpoint__c.
  3. The response updates QuoteLineItem.Net_Unit_Price__c and Discount_Percent__c.
  4. QuoteCalculatorService recomputes line and quote totals.
apex
public inherited sharing class PriceRuleEngineService {

    public static void applyExternalPrices(List<QuoteLineItem> lines) {
        HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest();
        req.setEndpoint('callout:PricingService/quote/price'); // Named credential
        req.setMethod('POST');
        req.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
        req.setBody(JSON.serialize(buildRequestPayload(lines)));

        Http http = new Http();
        HttpResponse res = http.send(req);

        if (res.getStatusCode() == 200) {
            PricingResponse parsed = PricingResponse.parse(res.getBody());
            for (Integer i = 0; i < lines.size(); i++) {
                lines[i].List_Unit_Price__c = parsed.lines.get(i).listPrice;
                lines[i].Net_Unit_Price__c = parsed.lines.get(i).netPrice;
                lines[i].Discount_Percent__c = parsed.lines.get(i).discountPct;
            }
        } else {
            throw new PricingResponse.PricingException(
                'Pricing service returned HTTP ' + res.getStatusCode());
        }
    }

    static String buildRequestPayload(List<QuoteLineItem> lines) {
        List<Map<String, Object>> payload = new List<Map<String, Object>>();
        for (QuoteLineItem li : lines) {
            payload.add(new Map<String, Object>{
                'productId' => li.Product2Id,
                'quantity' => li.Quantity,
                'configuredBundle' => li.Is_Bundle_Parent__c,
                'option' => li.Bundle_Option__c
            });
        }
        return JSON.serialize(payload);
    }
}

Governor-boundary rule: callouts are not allowed inside a transaction that has already done SOQL/DML unless you use async Apex (Queueable, future). Keep callouts in their own execution context: a Queueable chained after the DML commit, or a platform-event subscriber.

json
{
  "endpoint": "callout:PricingService/quote/price",
  "payload": [
    { "productId": "01tXX0000000000", "quantity": 10,
      "configuredBundle": true, "option": "Platinum" }
  ],
  "expected": { "listPrice": 100, "netPrice": 80, "discountPct": 20 }
}

Building an end-to-end sync with retries

Robust integrations survive transient outages. The Revenue_Sync__e fields support exactly that contract:

apex
public inherited sharing class OrderFulfillmentService {

    public static void syncToErp(Id orderId) {
        Order ord = [SELECT Id, ERP_Order_Number__c, Fulfillment_Status__c,
                            Total_ARR__c FROM Order WHERE Id = :orderId];

        Revenue_Sync__e evt = new Revenue_Sync__e(
            Source_Object__c = 'Order',
            Payload__c = JSON.serialize(ord),
            Direction__c = 'Outbound',
            Status__c = 'Pending',
            Correlation_Id__c = 'ERP-' + orderId,
            Retry_Count__c = 0,
            Endpoint__c = 'callout:ErpService/orders'
        );
        EventBus.publish(evt);
    }

    // Subscriber, called by the platform-event flow after the callout succeeds
    public static void markFulfilled(Id orderId, String erpNumber) {
        Order ord = new Order(Id = orderId);
        ord.Fulfillment_Status__c = 'Fulfilled';
        ord.Fulfillment_Date__c = Date.today();
        ord.ERP_Order_Number__c = erpNumber;
        update ord;
    }
}

The retry loop lives in the subscriber: if the callout fails, re-publish the same event with Retry_Count__c + 1 and the same Correlation_Id__c; the consumer treats repeated Correlation_Id__c as idempotent and only updates records once.

Flow version of the same path:

text
[Platform Event trigger] Revenue_Sync__e
  -> Decision: Status__c == 'Pending' and Retry_Count__c < 5
  -> External Service step: POST Payload__c to Endpoint__c
  -> On success: OrderFulfillmentService.markFulfilled(orderId, resp.id)
  -> On failure: Publish follow-up event, Retry_Count__c = old + 1
Tip: Put the retry budget (max retries, backoff) in a Custom Setting/Metadata so ops can tune it without a deploy.

Orchestration recipe: quote to fulfilled order

Combining everything in one scenario:

  1. Trigger: QuoteTriggerHandlerService runs on quote update.
  2. Flow: when Approval_Status__c becomes Approved, call ContractGenerationService to build the contract, then OrderFulfillmentService to publish the Revenue_Sync__e.
  3. Platform event subscriber (Flow or Apex) performs the ERP callout using named-credential callout:ErpService.
  4. Success flips CPQ_Sync_Status__c to Synced and marks the order Fulfilled.
  5. Failure re-publishes with a bumped Retry_Count__c, and a scheduled job or dashboard surfaces stuck Pending events.

Because every step is an Apex service with a single responsibility, the whole pipeline is unit-testable with @IsTest mocks for the callouts.

Warning: Never put credentials in callout URLs. Add the endpoint to a named credential, test with Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, ...), and keep the external system's auth in the credential, not in Apex.

Hands-on walkthrough

This mirrors exercises 12.1 (Publish and Subscribe to a Platform Event) and 12.2 (Call an External Pricing API).

  1. Create the Revenue_Sync__e platform event if it does not already exist (fields from the spec).
  2. Build Trigger Handler Framework: a QuoteTrigger entering through QuoteTriggerHandlerService.
  3. In QuoteTriggerHandlerService, add an AFTER_UPDATE branch that publishes a Revenue_Sync__e for every quote whose Approval_Status__c transitioned to Approved, with Correlation_Id__c derived from the quote Id.
  4. Create a Platform-Event-triggered Flow that fires on Revenue_Sync__e when Integration_Type__c == 'QuoteToERP', reads Payload__c, and calls the external pricing / ERP endpoint stored in Endpoint__c.
  5. Write PriceRuleEngineService.applyExternalPrices(lines) to POST the JSON payload above and parse the response.
  6. In the subscriber flow, on HTTP 200, call OrderFulfillmentService.syncToErp(orderId), then update Quote.CPQ_Sync_Status__c = 'Synced'.
  7. On HTTP failure, re-publish with Retry_Count__c incremented and the same Correlation_Id__c.
  8. Write an @IsTest that inserts a Quote, approves it, Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, ...) the pricing callout, and asserts the line's Net_Unit_Price__c matches the mock response.
  9. Add a SOQL guard: confirm the event subscriber did one update per Correlation_Id__c (absence of duplicates = idempotency).
  10. Finally, run the flow against a made-up order and confirm Fulfillment_Status__c and ERP_Order_Number__c land on the order.
apex
@IsTest
static void externalPricing_appliesNetPrice() {
    Quote q = TestQuoteFactory.build(); // quote + two lines
    insert q;

    PriceRuleEngineServiceMock mock = new PriceRuleEngineServiceMock(
        '{"lines":[{"listPrice":100,"netPrice":80,"discountPct":20},'
        + '{"listPrice":50,"netPrice":45,"discountPct":10}]}'
    );
    Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mock);

    Test.startTest();
    PriceRuleEngineService.applyExternalPrices(q.QuoteLineItems);
    Test.stopTest();

    Assert.areEqual(80, q.QuoteLineItems[0].Net_Unit_Price__c);
}

Common pitfalls

  • Burying logic in the trigger body instead of a handler; every future change rewrites the trigger.
  • Publishing payloads that omit fields, forcing subscribers to hit the database again.
  • Using an event Id as a correlation key, which breaks idempotency on retries.
  • Performing HTTP callouts after DML in the same transaction and hitting the "callout not allowed" limit.
  • Hard-coding callout endpoints instead of named credentials.
  • Ignoring Retry_Count__c, so a dead ERP client re-publishes forever.
  • Building a 100-element Flow because "flows are easier", when a 20-line Apex service would be trivial to test.

Key takeaways

  • Flows orchestrate; Apex computes and talks to the outside world.
  • QuoteTriggerHandlerService keeps triggers thin and lets every stage of quote-to-cash be invoked from Flow or Apex.
  • Revenue_Sync__e is your integration spine: Correlation_Id__c for idempotency, Retry_Count__c for resilience.
  • Callouts belong in their own transaction context and always through named credentials.
  • Every service should be reachable from Flow (invocable) so admins can adapt without code.
  • The same patterns run against RLM core objects, so skills transfer between engines.
